title: Oxygen Uptake Is Flow Times Extraction

scenes.tts: Take a healthy young man of about seventy kilograms. At rest, he takes up about two hundred fifty millilitres of oxygen per minute. At the end of a maximal run, he may take up ten or more times as much. That oxygen passes through the lungs, the heart, the blood and the capillaries before a mitochondrion uses it. Which link sets the ceiling?
scenes.visual: Two bars, rest and maximal run (open top); a vertical chain lungs, heart, blood, capillaries, mitochondrion fills in with question marks; a dashed ceiling line over the tall bar.
scenes.caption: Take a healthy young man of about 70 kg. At rest, he takes up about 250 mL of oxygen per minute. At the end of a maximal run, he may take up ten or more times as much. scenes.tts: Fick's principle splits the rise into two factors. Oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times the oxygen extracted from each litre of blood. That extraction is arterial oxygen content minus mixed-venous oxygen content, in millilitres of oxygen per litre of blood. Take illustrative numbers at rest: cardiac output is five litres per minute, and extraction is fifty millilitres per litre. Five times fifty gives two hundred fifty millilitres per minute.
scenes.visual: Axes: cardiac output (width) and extraction (height). The rest rectangle grows; its area is oxygen uptake.
scenes.caption: Fick's principle splits the rise into two factors. Oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times the oxygen extracted from each litre of blood. That extraction is arterial oxygen content minus mixed-venous oxygen content, in mL of oxygen per L of blood. Take illustrative numbers at rest: cardiac output is 5 L per minute, and extraction is 50 mL per L. Five times 50 gives 250 mL per minute.

scenes.tts: Now the same man at maximal exercise, with illustrative numbers. Heart rate is one hundred ninety-five beats per minute, and stroke volume is one hundred millilitres per beat. Cardiac output reaches nineteen and a half litres per minute, a rise of three point nine times. Extraction rises to one hundred sixty millilitres per litre, a rise of three point two times. Together they make oxygen uptake twelve and a half times its resting value.
scenes.visual: Rest rectangle stretched wider by 3.9 then taller by 3.2 into the maximal rectangle; numbers on the right.
scenes.caption: Now the same man at maximal exercise, with illustrative numbers. Heart rate is 195 beats per minute, and stroke volume is 100 mL per beat. Cardiac output reaches 19.5 L per minute, a rise of 3.9 times. Extraction rises to 160 mL per L, a rise of 3.2 times. Together they make oxygen uptake 12.5 times its resting value.

scenes.tts: Which factor sets the ceiling? Andersen and Saltin had five healthy subjects kick one leg, so the active muscle was essentially one quadriceps. Flow to that leg rose with workload to an average of five point seven litres per minute. They estimated maximal perfusion at about two and a half litres per kilogram of active muscle per minute. This did not test whole-body exercise.
scenes.visual: One working leg and one resting leg; cold-saline flow measurement in the working leg; the 5.7 L/min and 2.5 L/kg/min numbers.
scenes.caption: Which factor sets the ceiling? Andersen and Saltin had five healthy subjects kick one leg, so the active muscle was essentially one quadriceps. Flow to that leg rose with workload to an average of 5.7 L per minute. They estimated maximal perfusion at about 2.5 L per kg of active muscle per minute. This did not test whole-body exercise.

scenes.tts: Suppose, with made-up values, that running uses twenty kilograms of muscle. Eighty percent of the heart's nineteen and a half litres per minute reaches it. If the one-leg rate applies to all of that muscle, it could accept fifty litres per minute. The heart sends fifteen point six. Muscle could accept three times what the heart delivers, so in this example the heart sets the ceiling.
scenes.visual: Two bars: muscle could accept 50 L/min, heart sends 15.6 L/min; ratio 3.2.

scenes.tts: In healthy people doing whole-body exercise at sea level, the evidence points to oxygen delivery, mainly cardiac output. One training study's authors report that returning red-cell volume to baseline brought peak oxygen uptake back to its pretraining level. But removing blood also lowers blood volume and preload, so it cannot separate oxygen-carrying capacity from volume. A later study found the gain preserved, so the result is not settled. Oxygen uptake is flow times extraction, and in whole-body exercise at sea level the evidence points mainly to flow.
